analysis.one_liner: Requires electricity suppliers to sell a rising share of clean energy, with credits, penalties, and bill-reduction funds.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing, markup, or vote in the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would set a federal clean energy standard requiring every retail electricity supplier to sell a growing percentage of clean power, reaching at least 90% by 2040 and 100% after that. Suppliers could meet the target by buying federal clean energy credits, documenting their own clean generation, or paying an alternative compliance payment of 3 cents per kilowatt-hour, which rises over time. Money from those payments and from civil penalties would fund state efficiency programs and electricity bill reductions for households earning under three times the poverty line.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary households benefit through cleaner air and lower emissions; the bill's own stated purpose includes hundreds of billions of dollars in domestic health and environmental benefits and saving tens of thousands of lives. Households below 300% of the poverty line would receive direct electricity bill reductions funded by supplier payments and penalties. Clean energy industries — solar, wind, geothermal, hydropower, nuclear, storage, and carbon capture — gain a guaranteed, growing market. Workers on projects funded by the bill must be paid prevailing wages under Davis-Bacon rules.

how_it_helps.text: Requires each retail electricity supplier to sell a rising percentage of clean energy — renewables, hydropower, nuclear, storage-dispatched power, qualified biomass, waste-to-energy, low-carbon fuels, and carbon-captured power — growing to at least 90% and then 100% of sales.
Establishes a national market in federal clean energy credits, where one credit equals one megawatt-hour of clean generation, letting the market find the cheapest clean resources.

Directs all alternative compliance payments and civil penalties into state programs for energy efficiency, clean energy deployment, and electricity bill reductions for households below 300% of the poverty line.
Requires prevailing wages (Davis-Bacon) on projects funded by the bill's state programs and Buy American compliance for those projects.
States the standard is designed to produce hundreds of billions of dollars in health and environmental benefits and save tens of thousands of lives by mid-century.

analysis.who_pays: Fossil-fuel generators — especially coal plants and gas plants without capture — lose the ability to sell unabated power into a standard they helped pay their way out of only at rising cost. Electric utilities bear compliance costs, which are typically passed to customers through rates. Households could see somewhat higher electricity bills, particularly where clean resources are expensive to build quickly.

drawbacks.text: Suppliers can comply entirely by paying an alternative compliance fee of 3 cents per kilowatt-hour, so in any given year the standard could be satisfied with money rather than new clean generation; the fee starts low relative to average retail prices.

The definition of clean energy includes qualified renewable biomass, waste-to-energy combustion, and gas power up to a carbon intensity of 0.4 metric tons per megawatt-hour, so gas plants and wood-burning facilities could earn credits, diluting the emissions benefit and drawing opposition from environmental groups concerned about biomass and waste combustion accounting.

Compliance costs would flow through utility rates, and while the bill includes bill-reduction funds for lower-income households, the National Academy of Sciences review the bill orders explicitly requires evaluating effects on electricity prices and demand, acknowledging ratepayer cost is a real risk.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill aims at a real public good — a near-zero-emission electric grid — with a market-based design and direct bill relief for lower-income households, which is a stronger consumer design than many climate bills. Its weaknesses are the low-cost compliance payment that lets suppliers buy their way out in a given year and a broad clean-energy definition that credits gas, biomass, and waste combustion, each of which could soften the emissions result. On balance the benefits to public health and long-run energy costs plausibly outweigh the ratepayer costs, but the escape hatches are significant and honest supporters should acknowledge them.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in May 2019, read twice, and referred to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee, which never held a hearing, markup, or vote on it before the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Sen. Tina Smith introduced the bill on May 8, 2019, joined by five Democratic cosponsors: Sens. Heinrich, Kaine, Whitehouse, and Schatz.
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Energy and Natural Resources; that was the final action of record.

The CRS summary confirms no action beyond introduction; the bill text shows a full design for a federal clean energy standard, a credit trading program, civil penalties, and a state bill-reduction program.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Fossil-fuel generators and electric utilities that would have faced federal clean energy compliance costs are better off; no standard ever took effect, and the status quo — unabated fossil generation and no federal clean energy requirement — continued through the end of the Congress.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Fossil generators and utilities without new rules

sides.party_line_note: All six Senate supporters were Democrats (the sponsor plus five cosponsors); no Republican cosponsored, and the bill died in a Republican-chaired committee without a hearing.

industries.note: The standard forces them to buy credits or pay an escalating fee for unabated fossil generation; their cost is the price of the cleaner air and emissions reductions the public gains. Gas plants can earn small partial credits, softening the hit somewhat.

industries.industry: Renewable energy developers (solar, wind, geothermal, hydropower)
industries.note: The standard creates a guaranteed, growing demand for their output and a national credit market to sell into, and their growth delivers the emissions and health benefits the bill targets.
Existing nuclear counts fully as clean energy at each supplier's baseline, locking existing reactors into the compliance system as a revenue source while the standard drives demand for clean credits.
They bear the compliance obligation and penalties, but can pass costs to ratepayers, buy credits, or pay the alternative compliance fee, so they face real costs yet retain flexibility.

The bill credits qualified waste-to-energy and renewable biomass as clean energy, giving these combustion facilities new revenue; the emissions accounting for them is contested, so their gain may or may not serve the public's clean-air interest.
